question.prompt: A box contains \(2\) pennies, \(4\) nickels and \(6\) dimes. Six coins are drawn without replacement, with each coin having an equal probability of being chosen. What is the probability that the value of the coins drawn is at least \(50\) cents?

solutions.explanation:
The value condition strongly restricts the number of dimes. With at most three dimes, even replacing every other drawn coin by a nickel would give at most \(3(10)+3(5)=45\) cents. Thus a successful draw contains four, five, or six dimes.

Treat the twelve physical coins as distinct. Their six-coin subsets are equally likely, since every subset can be drawn in the same \(6!\) orders. There are \(\binom{12}{6}=924\) such subsets.

Count the successful subsets in three disjoint cases:

If all six coins are dimes, there is \(1\) subset.

If five coins are dimes, the remaining coin can be any of the six pennies and nickels. Even a penny makes the value \(51\) cents, so there are \(\binom65\cdot6=36\) subsets.

If four coins are dimes, the remaining two must both be nickels to reach \(50\) cents. There are \(\binom64\binom42=15\cdot6=90\) subsets.

These cases include every successful draw, and their different numbers of dimes prevent double counting. Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{1+36+90}{924}=\boxed{\frac{127}{924}},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
solutions.title: Count by the number of dimes
